sentences.text: Ohmdenosaurus was a primitive sauropod dinosaur that lived in what is now Germany during the Early Jurassic epoch. It was an obligate quadruped with a relatively short neck and a robust body.
Possessing quadrupedal locomotion and columnar limbs, this animal was one of the earliest known sauropods. Rupert Wild estimated the total body length of Ohmdenosaurus at 3 to 4 meters.

The only known specimen consists of a tibia measuring approximately 405 mm in length and an estimated femur of at least 70 cm. This tibia and ankle bones were found in the Posidonia Shale near Ohmden.

The tibia preserves muscle attachment sites, including a cnemial crest projecting about 4 cm and a crista lateralis running about 13 cm. The medial condyle of the tibia is significantly larger than the broken lateral condyle and sits 2 to 3 cm lower. The calcaneus is circular, measuring 43 mm in diameter and 15 mm in height.

Rupert Wild identified several small elements between 5 and 30 mm in size below the tibia's lateral condyle as cartilage. He argued that small elements near the Achilles tendon attachment site may represent sesamoids due to the high stress experienced in that area.
It is the only dinosaur identified from the Posidonia Shale.
The estimated total body length of 4 meters is relatively small for a sauropod.
A re-evaluation suggests a body length of 6.7 meters and a weight of 1.3 tonnes.

German paleontologist Rupert Wild identified the remains as a sauropod in the 1970s. He formally described the fossil as a new genus and species, Ohmdenosaurus liasicus, in 1978. Its fossils were originally described as plesiosaur remains until a 1978 review of the holotype identified them as sauropod fossils.
The name Ohmdenosaurus is derived from the village of Ohmden and the Greek word for lizard. The species was named Ohmdenosaurus liasicus by Wild in a 1978 publication.
Remains were recovered from the Posidonienschiefer in Baden-Württemberg, Germany, in 1978.

Ohmdenosaurus was a terrestrial animal whose fossil was transported at least 100 km from the shoreline before burial. Wear marks on the disarticulated bones suggest the animal died on land before its remains were washed into the sea and buried.
Ohmdenosaurus belongs to the parent group Sauropoda. Ohmdenosaurus is classified in the class Saurischia.
The genus authority is Wild, 1978. The species authority is Wild, 1978.
One study concluded that Ohmdenosaurus was a eusauropod. The non-convex shape of the astragalus suggests Ohmdenosaurus was a very basal sauropod.
Ohmdenosaurus lived during the early Toarcian age. The fossil dates to the early Toarcian, approximately 182 million years ago.
The fossil dates to the early Toarcian, approximately 182.0 to 175.6 million years ago.
It lived on a series of islands in what is now the Bohemia region. The nearest landmass was probably the Black Forest Massif about 100 km to the southwest.
It is debated whether the small elements near the ankle are sesamoids or calcified pieces of the astragalus cartilage.
Recent discoveries suggest Ohmdenosaurus may be less basal than previously thought and more closely related to gravisaurs.
